source.citation: Britannica, Bamum, and the Centre for African Music and Dance article on the Museum of the Bamoun Kings. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.founded: 1394, by the Tikar prince Nshare Yèn (Nchare), who settled in the region and built the palace at Foumban.
attributes.capital: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
attributes.title_of_ruler: King (mfon), a hereditary position. The ruler is also called Sultan.
attributes.continuity: The monarchy has survived through about 20 reigns. One source calls the present king the 19th monarch.
attributes.reigning_king: Mouhammad Nabil Mforifoum Mbombo Njoya, from 2021, according to one source.
attributes.craft: The Bamum are noted craftsmen. King Njoya's palace had 300 looms and six dye pits.
attributes.week: King Mônjù (1461 to 1498) introduced an eight-day week.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Ibrahim Njoya (CC BY-SA 4.0), Britannica, Bamum, AFP via the Philippine Daily Inquirer, and the Conversation article on the Museum of the Bamoun Kings (allAfrica). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.known_as: The most celebrated of the Bamum kings.
attributes.inventions: The Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku) around 1896, the Shümom language in 1912, and a corn-grinding machine.
attributes.religion: Founded a hybrid belief called Nwet-Nkwete, mixing Islam, Christianity and animist beliefs.
attributes.palace: Built the Foumban palace, completed in 1917.
attributes.exile: Exiled by the French authorities in 1931. He died in 1933.

source.citation: Africa History Extra, The invention of writing in an African kingdom, Britannica, Bamum, and AFP. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.inventor: King Ibrahim Njoya, with the help of at least two royal advisers, Nji Mama Pekekue and Adjia Nji-Gboron.
attributes.invented: Around 1895 or 1896. The first version, called Lerewa or Lewa, was completed around 1897.
attributes.size: Over 500 syllabic signs. Britannica counts 510 pictographic characters in the first system.
attributes.development: The script evolved through six stages between 1897 and 1931.
attributes.use: Thousands of works were written in it, from official letters and school texts to epics and court records.
attributes.origin_story: Njoya was inspired to create writing after a revelatory dream.
attributes.related_language: The Shümom language, introduced by Njoya in 1912.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Foumban Royal Palace (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the Plizio and Sygic travel pages. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.location: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
attributes.style: Shows influences from German colonial buildings.
attributes.use: The seat of the Kingdom of Bamum, where the king still lives.
attributes.unesco: On Cameroon's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list, since 2006 according to one source.
attributes.museum: The palace museum tells the history of the Bamum kings from 1394 to today.

source.citation: AFP via the Philippine Daily Inquirer and TRT World, the Conversation article on the Museum of the Bamoun Kings (allAfrica), and Urdu Point. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.collection: About 12,500 pieces, including weapons, pipes, musical instruments, a beaded royal stool, masks, costumes, King Njoya's manuscripts and the corn-grinding machine he invented.
attributes.building: Construction was launched in 2013 by King Ibrahim Mbombo Njoya, because the palace rooms were too small. Only a few of the pieces had been shown in the palace before.
attributes.entrance: Visitors pass under a large two-headed snake from the royal coat of arms.

source.citation: AFP via the Philippine Daily Inquirer, and Investir au Cameroun. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

content.name: Nguon rites of the Bamoun people

attributes.description: A set of rituals celebrated in a popular annual festival in Foumban.
attributes.unesco: Added to UNESCO's List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, months before the Museum of the Bamoun Kings opened in 2024. AFP calls them the Bamoun people, while one other news article calls them Bamiléké.
